extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, students of literature/theatre, and scholars of comedy/humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and practical guidance for creating and recognising comic character-types in drama and comedy, focusing on what makes a trait laughable, how types differ from tragic individuals, and the social function of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generality of comedy vs. individuality of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Altogether different is the object of comedy. Here it is in the work itself that the generality lies... Comedy depicts characters we have already come across and shall meet with again. It takes note of similarities. It aims at placing types before our eyes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use characters as representatives of classes/types rather than unique, unrepeatable individuals. Comedy should foreground traits that can be generalized and recognised across multiple people (types), whereas tragic art focuses on unique inner individuality. Examples: Le Misanthrope, L'Avare — titles that indicate classes; contrast with tragic heroes who are unique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation method for comedy: external, inductive, and generalising
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic observation is “directed outwards... Settling on the surface, it will not be more than skin-deep... In a word, method and object are here of the same nature as in the inductive sciences... observation is always external and the result always general.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating comic material, observe others' external behaviours and recurring surface patterns; abstract and generalise analogous cases to form a type. Avoid seeking deep causal, inner-life explanations for comic traits — surface regularities are the productive material for comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic trait source: absent‑mindedness / parasitic attribute
rubrics_metrics.description: “A person is never ridiculous except through some mental attribute resembling absent‑mindedness, through something that lives upon him without forming part of his organism, after the fashion of a parasite.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify behaviours or mental quirks that feel like foreign attachments (mechanical habits, incongruous impulses) rather than core, integrated aspects of personality. These parasitic attributes are visible to others (not to the person) and are prime sources of laughability because they can be observed and corrected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of an ideal comic type
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal comic type “must be deep‑rooted, so as to supply comedy with inexhaustible matter, and yet superficial, in order that it may remain within the scope of comedy; invisible to its actual owner, ... visible to everybody else; extremely considerate to its own self, ... troublesome to others; immediately repressible, ... sure of reappearing under fresh aspects, ... inseparable from social life, although insufferable to society; capable ... of being tacked on to all the vices and even to a good many virtues.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for traits that are (a) persistent enough to yield repeated comic situations, (b) shallow enough that exposure doesn't destroy the effect, (c) unconscious to the character but obvious to others, (d) socially embedded so they recur in contexts and among many people, and (e) flexible enough to appear in varied situations or attached to different moral qualities. This long checklist describes what makes a trait both reliably funny and useful dramatistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity as central comic element; laughter as remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: “This mixture is vanity... It is scarcely a vice, and yet all the vices are drawn into its orbit... the specific remedy for vanity is laughter, and that the one failing that is essentially laughable is vanity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vanity is a rich, widespread source of comic material: characters who overvalue themselves or are preoccupied with social admiration invite laughter. Comedy often functions socially to puncture vanity; structuring scenes to expose self‑admiration can fulfill comedy's corrective role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional comic: ready‑made categories (professional vanity and callousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: “There are ready-made categories established by society... the various trades, public services and professions... In the forefront we find professional vanity... Another form ... is what may be called professional callousness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professions supply recognisable, repeatable character-types (the pedant, the doctor, the judge, the merchant). Emphasise occupational habits, solemnity, claimed priesthood, or callousness that arise from professional roles as a shortcut to typification and recognisability. Examples given: Molière’s doctors, Labiche’s timber merchant, Perrin Dandin the judge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of repetition and satellites to define a type
rubrics_metrics.description: “The comic poet... impels the comic poet... to cause other characters, displaying the same general traits, to revolve as satellites round him... many comedies have a plural noun or collective term as their title.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate a type by presenting multiple similar characters (copies/varieties) rather than only a single example. Showing variations and repetitions helps audiences abstract the underlying type and recognise it as general rather than unique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization of comic cause: avoid deep causal explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: “To penetrate too far into the personality, to couple the outer effect with causes that are too deep-seated, would mean to endanger and in the end to sacrifice all that was laughable in the effect. In order that we may be tempted to laugh at it, we must localise its cause in some intermediate region of the soul.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not explain or justify comic behaviour by deep psychology or tragic backstory; keep the cause in an intermediate, surface-level zone that makes the behaviour appear average and correctable. Anti-pattern: reconceptualising a comic trait as a tragic wound, which diminishes laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy’s social function: corrective and reintegrative
rubrics_metrics.description: “The business of laughter is to repress any separatist tendency. Its function is to convert rigidity into plasticity, to readapt the individual to the whole, in short, to round off the corners wherever they are met with.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat comedy as social critique with the aim of adjusting behaviour: comedic exposure should point toward reintegration (correcting vanity or rigid quirks) rather than merely humiliating. Structuring comedy to highlight social re‑adaptation will align it with the essay’s theorised purpose of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles and naming as indicators of type
rubrics_metrics.description: “The very titles of certain classical comedies are significant in themselves. Le Misanthrope, l’Avare, le Joueur, le Distrait, etc., are names of whole classes of people... we say ‘a Tartuffe,’ but we should never say ‘a Phèdre’.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When labeling characters or plays, use names or epithets that connote types (collective nouns or stock labels) to signal generality. This helps audiences abstract the character into a recognisable social type.
